title: Months 4 to 6: The Second Trimester
learningGoals: Know how fast your baby grows in the second trimester
Know when many people first feel their baby move, and what it feels like
Know what the anatomy ultrasound checks and when it usually happens
Know where pregnancy weight gain goes, and that a healthy range depends on your weight before pregnancy

review.notes: Clinically reviewed 2026-10-25 by Bryan Kurtz MD, FACOG, who confirmed every source against its slides. Draft 2026-10-24 for the new How Your Baby Grows module, built around the March of Dimes month-by-month videos. Needs clinical review and every source confirmed against its slides. Sizes are rounded averages from ACOG's Changes During Pregnancy infographic. First movements are given as roughly 16 to 22 weeks, earlier in a later pregnancy; the anatomy ultrasound as about 18 to 22 weeks; hearing as "by the end of this trimester". Reviewer to confirm these ranges, and that ACOG supports the round ligament pain and fundal height lines on the body slide. Pictures are the reviewer's fetal and maternal development illustrations from the Pregnancy AI Assistant, padded to the class's 16:10 frame; that draft labeled the earliest stages in weeks after conception, while this class counts from the last period, so the pictures are placed by what they show. Draft 2026-10-30 at the reviewer's request: added 'Where the weight goes' (a breakdown table), 'What's right for you' (2009 IOM ranges by pre-pregnancy BMI, as used by ACOG and CDC; no BMI numbers shown, encouraging framing, no dieting unless advised), and a check-in, plus a summary line. For the reviewer: the breakdown figures are the commonly cited rounded values (secondary sources; not found on an approved page), the ranges are 25-35 normal, 28-40 underweight, 15-25 overweight, 11-20 obese, and the three new sources and their URLs need verifying.

slides.heading: Months 4 to 6: The Second Trimester
onScreen: How Your Baby Grows
slides.narration: Welcome back. This lesson covers the second trimester, months four to six. For many people, this is when pregnancy starts to feel real. Your baby grows fast, and somewhere in these months you'll likely feel the first little movements. We'll also talk about the anatomy ultrasound, a closer look at how your baby is growing.

visual.description: Side view cross-section of a pregnant body early in the second trimester, the uterus rising above the pubic bone with the baby curled inside.

slides.heading: Growing fast
onScreen: At 16 weeks: more than 4 inches, more than 3 ounces
At 20 weeks: more than 6 inches, under 11 ounces
Fine hair and a waxy coating protect the skin
Eyebrows and eyelashes grow
slides.narration: In the second trimester, your baby grows quickly. At sixteen weeks, your baby is more than four inches long and weighs a little over three ounces. By twenty weeks, your baby is more than six inches long. Fine, soft hair and a waxy, creamy coating cover and protect the skin. Eyebrows and eyelashes grow in. And your baby practices sucking and swallowing.

visual.description: Illustration of a fetus at about fourteen weeks, floating in the amniotic sac with the umbilical cord.

slides.heading: Feeling your baby move
onScreen: Often between about 16 and 22 weeks
Earlier if you've been pregnant before
Flutters, bubbles, or a gentle tap
Not every day at first, and that's normal
slides.narration: Many people first feel their baby move somewhere between about sixteen and twenty-two weeks. If you've been pregnant before, you may notice it sooner. Early movements are gentle. People describe them as flutters, bubbles, or a light tap. At first, you won't feel them every day, and that's normal. The kicks get stronger and more regular as your baby grows.

visual.description: Illustration of a fetus at about twenty weeks, arms and legs bent, moving inside the uterus.

slides.heading: The anatomy ultrasound
onScreen: Usually around 18 to 22 weeks
Checks your baby's body and organs
Checks the placenta and amniotic fluid
You can often learn the sex, if you want to
slides.narration: Many people have an ultrasound around eighteen to twenty-two weeks. It's often called the anatomy scan. Your care team uses it to look at your baby's body and organs, check how your baby is growing, and see where the placenta is and how much fluid surrounds your baby. You can often learn your baby's sex at this scan, if you'd like to know. If something needs a closer look, your care team will talk with you about next steps.

slides.heading: Your baby is listening
onScreen: Hearing develops in this trimester
Your baby can hear your heartbeat and your voice
Sleep and wake times begin
slides.narration: By the end of the second trimester, your baby can hear. Your heartbeat, your digestion, and your voice are part of your baby's world. Some parents like to talk, read, or sing to their baby. Your baby also starts to have times of sleep and times of being awake and active.

slides.heading: Your body: months 4 to 6
onScreen: Your belly starts to show
By about 20 weeks, the top of your uterus reaches your belly button
Your care team may measure your belly to check growth
Brief, sharp pains low on the sides are common as it stretches
Practice contractions may start
slides.narration: In the second trimester, your belly starts to show. Your uterus rises out of your pelvis, and by about twenty weeks, the top of it reaches your belly button. At your visits, your care team may measure from your pubic bone to the top of your uterus to check that your baby is growing. As the uterus stretches, you may feel brief, sharp pains low on one or both sides when you move quickly. You may also notice your belly tightening now and then. These practice contractions, called Braxton Hicks, are usually irregular and go away. If they become regular or painful before thirty-seven weeks, call your care team.

visual.description: Side view cross-section of a pregnant body at about twenty weeks: the top of the uterus is level with the belly button, and the intestines are pushed up and to the sides.

slides.heading: Where the weight goes
onScreen: Most of what you gain is your baby and the support your body builds for them
Only part of it is stored fat, and that's fuel for feeding your baby
slides.narration: It can feel strange to watch the scale go up. So let's look at where the weight actually goes. Your baby is only part of it, about seven to eight pounds at birth. The placenta weighs a pound or two, and the amniotic fluid around your baby is about two pounds more. Your uterus grows from the size of a pear to hold all of it, adding about two pounds. Your breasts grow as they get ready to make milk. Your blood volume rises a lot, to carry oxygen to your baby, and your body holds extra fluid too. And some is stored energy, which your body uses after birth, especially if you breastfeed. Put together, nearly all of it is your body doing exactly what it should.

slides.heading: What's right for you
onScreen: How much to gain depends on your weight before pregnancy
A common range is 25 to 35 pounds; yours may be higher or lower
Most of the gain comes in the second and third trimesters
Eat well, stay active, and don't diet during pregnancy unless your care team advises it
Ask your care team what range is right for you
slides.narration: How much weight is healthy to gain depends on where you started before pregnancy. For many people, the range is twenty-five to thirty-five pounds. If you started at a lower weight, it may be a little more. If you started at a higher weight, it may be less, often fifteen to twenty-five, or eleven to twenty pounds. Expecting twins? It's more. Most of the gain comes in the second and third trimesters, a little at a time. Eating a variety of healthy foods and staying active help you gain at a steady pace. This isn't the time to diet, unless your care team suggests it. Your care team will track your weight at each visit, and they can tell you the range that's right for you. And if the number on the scale worries you, say so. It's a great thing to talk about together.

slides.heading: Quick check-in
slides.narration: Let's pause for a quick check-in.

question.prompt: Your baby will weigh about 7 to 8 pounds at birth, but you've gained more than that. Where does the rest go?
options: Your placenta, amniotic fluid, a larger uterus, breast tissue, extra blood and fluid, and stored energy
Mostly water that you should try to cut back on
question.explanation: Most of what you gain is your baby and the support your body builds for them: the placenta, amniotic fluid, a larger uterus, breast tissue, extra blood and fluid, and some stored energy for feeding.

slides.heading: Quick check-in
slides.narration: Let's pause for a quick check-in.

question.prompt: You're 17 weeks into your first pregnancy and haven't felt your baby move yet. What's true?
options: That's common. Many people first feel movement between about 16 and 22 weeks
Babies don't move until the third trimester
question.explanation: First movements often come between about sixteen and twenty-two weeks, and later in a first pregnancy. If you have questions, ask at your next visit.

slides.heading: What we covered
onScreen: Your baby grows fast: more than 6 inches by 20 weeks
First movements: often 16 to 22 weeks
The anatomy ultrasound: around 18 to 22 weeks
Weight gain is mostly your baby and the support your body builds
Your baby can hear your voice
slides.narration: Let's recap. In the second trimester, your baby grows quickly, to more than six inches long by twenty weeks. Many people feel their baby's first flutters between about sixteen and twenty-two weeks. The anatomy ultrasound, around eighteen to twenty-two weeks, checks how your baby is growing. Most of the weight you gain is your baby and the support your body builds for them, and your care team can tell you the range that's right for you. And by the end of these months, your baby can hear your voice. Next, a few review questions. Then on to the final stretch, months seven to nine.

reviewQuiz.prompt: What does the anatomy ultrasound check?
options: Your baby's body, growth, the placenta and the fluid
Only whether it's a boy or a girl
reviewQuiz.explanation: Around eighteen to twenty-two weeks, the anatomy ultrasound checks your baby's body and organs, growth, the placenta and the amniotic fluid. Learning the sex is optional.

reviewQuiz.prompt: What do early movements often feel like?
options: Strong kicks you can see from outside
Flutters, bubbles, or a light tap
reviewQuiz.explanation: Early movements are gentle, like flutters or bubbles. They get stronger as your baby grows.
